title: Trump Claims He Reversed Biden EV Rule, Boosting Updated Fuel Economy Standards
body:
President Donald Trump used a Saturday briefing to announce that his administration has rolled back the electric‑vehicle (EV) mandate embedded in the 2024 fuel‑economy standards, replacing it with a revised rule that focuses on traditional gasoline‑engine efficiency. The move eliminates the requirement that a growing share of new cars sold in the United States be electric—a cornerstone of President Joe Biden’s climate agenda—and signals a sharp shift in federal transportation policy toward lower‑cost, internal‑combustion technologies.

The revised standards, which were signed into effect by the Department of Transportation and the Environmental Protection Agency under Trump’s direction, retain the overall target for average fuel‑economy improvements but drop the specific 50 percent EV sales goal that had been slated for 2032. Instead, manufacturers will now be measured primarily on incremental gains in miles per gallon (MPG) for gasoline and hybrid models, with a modest credit system for plug‑in hybrids that do not meet full‑electric criteria. The administration argues that the new rule will “protect American workers,” curb “unnecessary regulatory burdens,” and keep vehicle prices affordable for consumers still reliant on gasoline.

Industry reaction has been mixed. Major automakers such as General Motors, Ford and Stellantis had already begun retooling factories and investing billions in battery production to meet the original EV quota. In a statement, the Alliance of Automobile Manufacturers welcomed the “predictability” of the revised standards but warned that the abrupt policy reversal could disrupt supply chains and lead to stranded investments in electric‑vehicle platforms. Conversely, the National Association of Manufacturers praised the decision, saying it restores “a level playing field” for firms that have long championed internal‑combustion efficiency improvements over costly battery development.

Environmental groups have condemned the rollback as a step backward for climate mitigation. The Sierra Club’s senior policy director called the action “a blatant abandonment of the United States’ commitments under the Paris Agreement,” noting that transportation accounts for roughly 30 percent of national greenhouse‑gas emissions. Analysts at the International Energy Agency warned that removing the EV mandate could delay the projected 2030 target of 30 percent electric‑vehicle sales, potentially increasing cumulative emissions by millions of tons of carbon dioxide over the next decade. Some state governments, notably California, have signaled they will continue to enforce their own stricter emissions rules, creating a patchwork of regulations that could complicate compliance for manufacturers operating across state lines.

The policy shift also carries significant financial implications. The U.S. Treasury estimates that the revised standards could save consumers an average of $1,200 per vehicle in upfront costs, as electric models typically command higher price tags. However, the same analysis projects a loss of roughly $5 billion in federal tax revenue from the EV tax credits that were slated to fund infrastructure and consumer incentives. Moreover, the rollback may affect the burgeoning domestic battery industry, which has attracted over $30 billion in private investment and aims to position the United States as a global leader in clean‑energy technology.

Looking ahead, the administration’s decision is likely to spark legal challenges and further debate in Congress. Lawmakers from both parties have introduced bills either to reinstate the original EV mandate or to codify the new standards into law, reflecting deep partisan divides over the nation’s energy transition. As automakers adjust production plans and states grapple with divergent regulations, the automotive market may experience a period of uncertainty that could influence consumer choices, investment flows, and the United States’ ability to meet its longer‑term climate goals. The coming months will reveal whether this policy reversal becomes a lasting pivot or a temporary reprieve in the broader push toward electrified transportation.
